title: Integrating Nutraceutical and Biotechnological Therapies for Retinal Neurodegeneration
summary: Neurodegenerative disorders present one of the most challenging fronts in modern medicine, with diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease impacting millions globally. These conditions are characterized by the progressive degeneration and death of nerve cells, which is a complex interplay of genetic, oxidative, and inflammatory factors. The conventional therapeutic strategies are often inadequate, mainly due to their inability to target multiple pathological pathways simultaneously. As such, there is a critical need for innovative approaches that address these limitations effectively. In addition to central nervous system disorders, neurodegenerative conditions affecting the retina, such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and retinitis pigmentosa (RP), represent significant challenges. These retinal neurodegenerations share common pathological mechanisms with other neurodegenerative diseases, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic inflammation.

summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a rapidly growing concern at the intersection of environmental microbiology and evolutionary developmental biology. The microbial resistome—the entire collection of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) in a microbiome—has emerged as a dynamic system profoundly influenced by human activities. Anthropogenic pressures such as agricultural intensification, pollution, and wastewater inputs reshape microbial habitats, prompting the development, recruitment, and spread of resistance traits. Recent studies highlight how developmental gene regulation, horizontal gene transfer, and ecological selection combine to drive both the evolutionary diversification of ARGs and the adaptation of microbial communities. Yet, despite advances in phylogenetics and molecular ecology, major gaps persist in linking the developmental origins of ARGs with their evolutionary trajectories and ecological outcomes under environmental transformation.

summary: The orexin/hypocretin system, first identified in 1998, is now recognized as a central regulator of energy balance, sleep–wake states, and arousal stability. Orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus integrate circadian, metabolic, and environmental signals to promote wakefulness and stabilize sleep–wake transitions. Beyond arousal regulation, orexin signaling plays a key role in hedonic and motivational processes, as these neurons densely innervate limbic and reward-related brain regions. Disruption of this system has been implicated in sleep disorders, including narcolepsy type 1, insomnia, and hypersomnia, as well as substance use disorders. Emerging evidence further links orexin dysfunction to neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative, and psychiatric conditions.

While several studies have pointed to overlapping reward and executive control circuits across diagnoses, critical questions remain about how these mechanisms interact, whether they follow a common trajectory, and how they can be reliably measured and targeted for intervention. title: Bamboo: The Green Gold of Ecosystems – A Multifaceted Approach to Climate Resilience
summary: Bamboo has emerged as a symbol of sustainable growth and environmental stewardship in recent years. Recognized for its rapid growth and remarkable ecological benefits, bamboo is increasingly being viewed as a keystone species for ecosystem restoration and climate resilience. Its natural properties, such as efficient carbon absorption and structural versatility, make it an attractive option for sustainable development initiatives. However, despite its potential, bamboo's role in ecological restoration and its economic advantages remain underexplored in the context of global climate strategies. Current research emphasizes the urgent need to understand how bamboo-centric approaches can be integrated into policy frameworks to foster ecological stability and enrich biodiversity.

title: Robotics & machine learning for understanding neural networks
summary: Biological neural networks are immensely complex systems underlying all aspects of cognition and behavior. Despite significant advances in neuroscience, a comprehensive understanding of their intricate computational principles remains a grand challenge. Concurrently, artificial neural networks (ANNs) and deep learning have revolutionized artificial intelligence, demonstrating impressive capabilities often inspired by biological architectures. However, translating insights from ANNs back to fundamental biological mechanisms is often non-trivial. Robotics offers a unique avenue to bridge this gap, providing embodied platforms to test computational models of neural function in dynamic, interactive environments. This Research Topic seeks to leverage the analytical power of machine learning and the experimental validation capabilities of robotics to gain deeper insights into the working principles of biological neural networks.

title: Virtual reality as a tool for cognitive and sensory modulation
summary: Virtual Reality (VR) has emerged as a transformative medium in neuroscience, moving beyond entertainment into a robust tool for experimental manipulation. Traditionally, studying cognitive and sensory processes required a trade-off between controlled laboratory settings and real-world ecological validity. VR bridges this gap by providing immersive, three-dimensional environments that can be precisely modulated to isolate specific neural responses. By engaging multiple sensory modalities—visual, auditory, and increasingly somatosensory—VR creates a sense of "presence" that activates the brain in ways traditional 2D stimuli cannot. This immersive capacity allows researchers to investigate how the human brain processes complex sensory inputs and orchestrates cognitive functions in real-time.

title: Mitophagy and Mitochondrial Quality Control in Brain Aging and Neurodegeneration

Disrupted clearance of damaged mitochondria contributes to oxidative stress, energy failure, inflammation, and protein aggregation, all of which are hallmarks of disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, and other age-related cognitive and motor syndromes.

Stroke Among Cancer Patients: Exploring Shared Pathways and Prognoses
summary: Neurological and oncological intersections are increasingly relevant in medical research due to rising survival rates from cancer, which inadvertently elevate the risk of associated complications such as strokes. Approximately one in ten ischemic stroke victims also suffer from concurrent cancer, a statistic anticipated to increase with the advancements in cancer treatments that prolong survival. Recent studies reveal an emergence of stroke within two years of a cancer diagnosis in an additional 3-5% of cases. These include strokes that coincide with specific cancer therapies like chemotherapy and radiation, which could augment stroke risk through various mechanisms, including the induction of hypercoagulable states. Moreover, certain cancers have shown a high propensity to cause vascular complications, thus exacerbating the likelihood of stroke.

summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a devastating secondary neuroinflammatory cascade—driven by microglial activation, immune infiltration, and sustained pro-inflammatory mediator release—that exacerbates tissue damage and impedes neurological recovery. The dynamic balance between pro-inflammatory (M1) and reparative (M2) phenotypes of microglia/macrophages has emerged as a critical determinant of injury outcome. Key signaling pathways, including NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, TLR4, and the CCL2/CCR2 axis, represent promising pharmacological targets. Despite encouraging preclinical advances, effective clinical translation remains limited. This Research Topic aims to bridge mechanistic insights into SCI neuroinflammation with innovative pharmacological interventions, fostering the development of targeted therapies that can ultimately improve functional recovery after SCI.

summary: Epilepsy affects over 50 million individuals globally and remains one of the most challenging neurological disorders to manage. Approximately one-third of people with epilepsy experience drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), for whom surgical interventions offer a vital alternative. When non-invasive presurgical evaluation fails to define the seizure onset zone, invasive testing is performed. While tools such as intracranial EEG recordings with stereo-electroencephalography (Stereo-EEG) and subdural electrodes are part of the presurgical evaluation for decades, recent advances are redefining how these modalities are applied, interpreted, and integrated into the presurgical evaluation and surgical planning.

title: Educators in the Digital Age: The Role of Technology, Pedagogy, and Social Factors in Online Learning
summary: Digital transformation in education is changing the role of educators, the nature of student engagement, and the quality of instruction, particularly within virtual and hybrid environments. With advancements in technology such as artificial intelligence, educational software, and learning analytics, the educational landscape is undergoing major changes. These changes are influencing not only how and what we learn but also who teaches, how they teach, and the competencies required. In this changing context, educators' roles extend beyond merely transmitting knowledge to becoming mentors, support systems, and guides in the digital age. From autonomous vehicles and aerial drones to robotic manipulators and assistive medical devices, the integration of adaptive, learning-based, and data-driven controllers has expanded the capabilities of these systems to function in highly dynamic contexts. title: Beyond Symptom Control - Mechanistic Lessons from Failed and Emerging Disease-Modifying Therapies in Parkinson’s Disease
summary: Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, yet despite decades of mechanistic insight, every clinical trial of a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) to date has failed to deliver unequivocal evidence of slowed neurodegeneration. Recent high-profile negative results — including trials of NLY01 (a GLP-1 receptor agonist targeting microglial activation) and deferiprone (an iron chelator targeting nigral iron accumulation and ferroptotic vulnerability) — have prompted a critical re-examination of the preclinical models, target validation strategies, and molecular hypotheses that underpin the DMT pipeline.

title: Social Isolation, Social Participation, and Health Outcomes in Older Adults
summary: Research on ageing populations increasingly highlights the profound effects of social connectedness on health and well-being in later life. Social isolation is recognized as a significant risk factor for a range of adverse health outcomes among older adults, including cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease, depression, and reduced quality of life. While social participation is frequently associated with more positive physical and psychological outcomes, the mechanisms linking these factors remain insufficiently explored. The rapid uptake of digital technology, particularly smartphones, introduces both opportunities and challenges to the social integration of older people. Despite a growing body of research, much of the current literature is fragmented and lacks a holistic view of how overlapping social, technological, and psychological variables interact to shape health trajectories among older adults.

summary: The human brain is a relentless processor of sensory information, yet only a small fraction of this input reaches the level of conscious awareness. By precisely controlling stimulus properties, through techniques such as masking, binocular rivalry, or continuous flash suppression, researchers can dissociate physical input from subjective experience. summary: Brain development is a complex, dynamic, and multiscale process that unfolds from early embryogenesis through adolescence and into early adulthood. Across this trajectory, tightly coordinated mechanisms, including neural proliferation, migration, differentiation, synaptogenesis, pruning, and activity-dependent plasticity, shape the structure and function of the mature brain. These processes emerge through nonlinear interactions between genetic programs, cellular dynamics, environmental influences, and experience.

title: Artificial Intelligence for the Prevention, Surveillance, and Control of Animal Infectious Diseases
summary: Animal infectious diseases remain a major threat to animal health and welfare, livestock and aquaculture sustainability, and public health through zoonotic risk. At the same time, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a powerful tool for advancing the understanding, prevention, and control of infectious diseases in animal populations. Machine learning and related data-driven approaches are increasingly being used to model pathogen transmission, identify environmental drivers of disease emergence, predict outbreak risk, optimize vaccination strategies, strengthen antimicrobial stewardship, and integrate complex epidemiological, immunological, genomic, and ecological datasets. These developments offer new opportunities to support more targeted, timely, and effective infectious disease management across production animals, companion animals, wildlife, and aquatic species. Design, Modeling, and Adaptive Control of Innovative Joints for Collaborative and Industrial Robotic Systems
summary: Robotic joints are indispensable components that directly determine the capabilities and performance of diverse robotic systems. In the domain of collaborative and assistive robots, adaptive joints are essential for enabling safe human-robot interaction, demanding compliance and adaptability to ever-changing environments. Current approaches employ soft actuators, variable stiffness mechanisms, and compliant transmission elements to enhance safety and operational efficiency. On the other hand, industrial robots necessitate joint designs that prioritize high precision, repeatability, and robustness. The intricate design of these joints balances compactness, reliability, and a broad spectrum of functional prerequisites, necessitating a multidisciplinary synthesis of expertise in mechanics, actuation systems, control algorithms, and materials science to deploy joints that not only function precisely but also adapt effectively to the specific demands of different robotic tasks.

title: Stratification and Predictive Biomarkers in Autism and Other Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Advancing EEG and Eye-Tracking Approaches to Optimize Intervention Strategies
summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and other neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are characterized by substantial heterogeneity in etiology, symptomatology, developmental course, and treatment response. This heterogeneity poses significant challenges for clinical practice and research, particularly in the design and evaluation of effective early interventions. Attempts to stratify children diagnosed with these conditions have been primarily based on behavioral criteria, but clinical subtyping operates without reference to the underlying neurobiological mechanisms and has limited predictive value of the forthcoming developmental path. To advance tailored interventions in ASD and other NDDs, there is a growing emphasis on the discovery and validation of biomarkers that can objectively identify clinically meaningful subgroups and predict intervention response.

Tenecteplase is rapidly replacing alteplase as the thrombolytic of choice in many systems following AcT, TRACE-2, and ATTEST-2. A Metaverse for the Good: AI and the Metaverse
summary: The idea of the metaverse is a vast extended reality set of worlds where physical and virtual reality intersect. It might be inhabited at any one time by millions of people, and as in the real world groups of people can interact with one another in real-time. title: Current Perspectives of The Neurobiology of Prosody and Rhythm
summary: Prosody and rhythm are core components of speech that allow the brain to transform acoustic signals into linguistic and affective meaning. The interplay of pitch, stress, timing, and intonation patterns conveys syntactic structure, emotion, and communicative intent, while rhythmic organization supports segmentation, prediction, and motor coordination. Recent neuroscience research has revealed that prosodic and rhythmic functions depend on distributed neural networks spanning auditory, motor, subcortical, and cerebellar regions, coordinated by oscillatory activity across temporal scales. Despite these advances, key questions remain about how these systems develop, how their dysfunction contributes to communication disorders, and how prosody interacts with music, movement, and emotion across contexts and languages. Bridging these knowledge gaps is essential to understand how the brain encodes the temporal and melodic contours that shape human speech.

title: Biofilms and antimicrobial resistance in livestock pathogens: mechanisms, detection and control
summary: Biofilms play a crucial role in the persistence and spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in livestock production systems. Pathogens affecting cattle, swine, and poultry often form biofilms on animal tissues and farm environments, increasing their tolerance to antimicrobials and host defenses. Advances in genomics, transcriptomics, and imaging have deepened our understanding of the molecular basis of biofilm formation and its link to horizontal gene transfer and resistome dynamics.This Research Topic aims to gather studies exploring the mechanisms, detection, and control of biofilm-associated AMR in veterinary pathogens. Emphasis will be placed on innovative strategies such as phage therapy, anti-biofilm peptides, quorum-sensing inhibitors, and nanomaterials. By integrating microbiology, veterinary medicine, and biotechnology, this collection seeks to provide new insights and practical solutions to mitigate biofilm-mediated resistance and promote sustainable animal production.

title: Know your rodent: Impact of rodent strain on learning, memory, cognition and animal models of brain disease
summary: The choice of rodent strain for neuroscientific research is often considered a secondary factor when selecting rat or mouse models for functional studies of the brain. The predominant backstrain for transgenic mice is the C57BL/6 mouse strain, which is also the most widely used strain in non-transgenic experiments. However, this mouse strain develops progressive deafness beginning in early postnatal life and also exhibits a variety of ocular dysfunctions that may influence behavioral outcomes. Other mouse strains display marked differences in learning propensity, emotionality, and cognitive performance, as well as variability in both the behavioral symptoms and mechanistic underpinnings of disease models. A similar pattern is observed in rats, whereby, for example, Albino strains exhibit differences in learning compared to pigmented rat strains, that may be associated with differences in excitation-inhibition balance derives from altered GABAergic regulation.

title: Innovative electrode and bioelectronic technologies for neural recording and stimulation
summary: Neuroengineering is an ever-evolving field that is transforming our understanding of the nervous system through the development of sophisticated electrode and bioelectronic technologies. Traditional neural electrodes face significant challenges in interface stability, biocompatibility, long-term signal fidelity, and resolution, which hinder their broader application in neuroscience research and brain–machine interfacing. Recent studies have introduced innovations such as flexible materials, nano-scale architectures, and minimally invasive designs that promise higher integration with neural tissues, reduced immune response, and improved longevity. Despite these advances, achieving seamless, durable, and high-resolution communication with neural circuits remains one of the central challenges in next-generation neural interfacing.

title: Novel Molecular and Cellular Targets Driving Axon Regeneration After Spinal Cord Injury
summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to devastating and often irreversible loss of sensory and motor function due to the limited regenerative capacity of the adult central nervous system. Axon regeneration, the ability of injured neurons to re-extend functional projections, is a critical prerequisite for restoring connectivity and neurological recovery. Despite decades of research, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern axon regeneration remain only partially understood. This Research Topic aims to highlight emerging molecular and cellular targets that drive axon regeneration following spinal cord injury. By integrating discoveries from transcriptomic profiling, genetic manipulation, and advanced imaging, this collection seeks to uncover new regulatory pathways and therapeutic strategies that promote axonal growth and synaptic reconnection after injury.

title: Innovative experimental platforms in neuroscience research: from development to application
summary: Neuroscience research has recently experienced a dramatic evolution facilitated by the advent of sophisticated experimental platforms that imitate the human brain's structural and functional intricacies. Traditionally, monoculture systems prevailed, but now there's a shift towards dynamic, integrative models that can replicate the interactions between various cell types, their developmental paths, and environmental signals. Revolutionary approaches such as 3D cell cultures, brain organoids, and microfluidic devices have emerged as pivotal tools, offering translationally pertinent environments for understanding disease mechanisms, modeling brain development, and evaluating therapeutic interventions with improved consistency and predictive potency.

Beyond convention: novel biologics – targeted therapies for neuroimmune diseases
summary: Neuroimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, and autoimmune encephalitis, are debilitating conditions characterized by an aberrant immune response against the nervous system. For decades, treatment has relied on broad-spectrum immunosuppressants, which, while effective for some, are often associated with significant side effects and increased infection risk due to their non-specific mechanisms. This has left a substantial unmet need for many patients. The field is now undergoing a transformation with the introduction of targeted therapies, including monoclonal antibodies against specific immune molecules (e.g., CD20, complement proteins) and small molecule inhibitors. These novel agents promise greater efficacy and precision. Furthermore, next-generation approaches like bispecific antibodies and CAR-T cell therapy are emerging, pushing the boundaries of precision medicine in neurology.

title: Synergistic Adaptation of Wetland Communities under Multiple Stressors
summary: The integrity and functioning of wetland ecosystems are sustained by dynamic, finely tuned interaction networks among their biological constituents. Plants, microorganisms, and waterbirds form the core of the wetland “living community,” serving respectively as primary producers, drivers of biogeochemical cycles, and higher-level consumers. This interconnected network responds to environmental variation through inherent synergistic and feedback processes that govern a wetland’s resilience to cumulative stressors and shape its long-term ecological trajectory.

Emerging evidence highlights mechanisms involving microbiota-derived metabolites, immune system modulation, and neural signaling pathways as principal routes through which the gut influences brain health and function. title: Recent Advances in the Stabilization and Integration of Associative Memories
summary: The potential to adapt our behavior in response to environmental demands relies on our ability to generate and update memories of relevant information. After learning, memories undergo consolidation, a process that strengthens memory traces and transforms them into stable, long-lasting forms. On a cellular level, learning triggers rapid posttranslational modifications, such as the synthesis of plasticity-related proteins, facilitating synapse formation and maturation. On the circuit level, various brain areas form networks crucial for learning and memory. The most studied is the one involving the hippocampus, neocortex, and limbic nuclei, which are essential for memory consolidation. According to system consolidation theory, memories are initially encoded by the hippocampus and later transferred to the neocortex. This idea has been backed by studies that reveal coordination between hippocampal reactivations and cortical oscillations during sleep.

Targeting Primary Aging Mechanisms in Neurodegenerative Disease
summary: Aging is the primary risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Despite extensive research on disease-specific mechanisms, emerging evidence suggests that fundamental aging processes, such as mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis impairment, genomic instability, and chronic inflammation, play a central role in disease onset and progression. As new research underscores their importance, these mechanisms present a vital target for developing new therapies that inhibit disease progression and preserve neural function. Recent technological advancements in in molecular biology, transcriptomics, and systems biology have furthered our understanding of the relationship between aging and neurodegeneration, paving the way for interventions aimed at delaying disease progression and preserving cognitive and motor functions.

title: Imaging-Guided Neuromodulation for Brain Cognitive Function Enhancement: Methodological Advances in Targeting, Biomarkers, and Validation
summary: Neuroimaging has become central to cognitive enhancement research, transforming non-invasive neuromodulation from an empirical practice into a mechanistically grounded discipline. Today, neuroregulatory technologies — including transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), TMS, neurofeedback, and emerging modalities such as tFUS and TIS — are routinely paired with fMRI, fNIRS, and EEG. This coupling shifts cognitive enhancement from behavioral observation toward mechanistic exploration: imaging defines cortical targets, monitors interventions in real time, and validates stimulation effects at the network level. Yet critical methodological gaps remain. Artifact contamination in simultaneous stimulation–imaging recordings, multi-site inconsistencies, limited reliability of imaging biomarkers, and weak causal links between stimulation, imaging changes, and cognitive outcomes all constrain reproducibility and individualization.

title: Surgical and Healthcare-Worker Neuroergonomics
summary: Healthcare is among the most cognitively demanding and high-stakes forms of skilled work. Surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses, intensive-care and emergency staff, and trainees must sustain attention, integrate complex information, make rapid decisions, and perform precise motor actions, often under time pressure, interruption, and fatigue. The consequences of momentary lapses can be severe for patients and clinicians alike. Neuroergonomics offers a powerful lens on these demands by measuring the brain and body at work, using electroencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, eye tracking, pupillometry, and wearable sensing to quantify the cognitive and physiological states of healthcare workers during real and simulated clinical tasks.

title: Freshwater Ecosystems Under Global Changes​​​​​​​
summary: Freshwater ecosystems, including rivers, lakes, ponds, and wetlands, play a critical role in sustaining biodiversity, regulating biogeochemical cycles, and providing services essential to human well-being. However, these systems are increasingly degraded by global environmental change and anthropogenic disturbances. Climate warming, urbanization, land-use transformation, and hydraulic engineering have collectively altered hydrological regimes, increased pollution levels, and undermined ecological balance. Recent studies demonstrate the accelerating loss of freshwater biodiversity and functional integrity, yet the interactive effects of multiple stressors remain insufficiently understood. This gap challenges efforts to predict ecological trajectories and design effective conservation responses. A deeper comprehension of ecosystem resilience mechanisms is therefore vital to guide restoration practices and promote adaptive management under ongoing global changes.

summary: The field of trauma and disaster psychology has increasingly emphasized post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) as one of the most critical and enduring mental health outcomes of natural catastrophes such as earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, and wildfires. These events profoundly disrupt lives and communities, often resulting in both immediate and long-term emotional distress that spans generations. As natural disasters become more frequent and severe due to climate change, there is growing recognition that trauma are not confined to any specific age group — children, adolescents, adults, and older individuals are all affected in unique yet interconnected ways. While humanitarian efforts often prioritize physical safety and reconstruction, mental health recovery remains under-addressed, calling for a more holistic approach to post-disaster care and research.

Despite this progress, real-world clinical care still faces significant hurdles, such as delayed diagnosis, misclassification of seizure types, and variability in the application of evidence-based treatments. Recent studies demonstrate substantial potential for tools like EEG biomarkers, computational models, and novel imaging techniques to enhance diagnostic and therapeutic precision. However, gaps persist in translating these innovations into routine clinical practice, particularly in diverse clinical environments and among vulnerable populations, leaving many patients without optimal care.

Extracellular Vesicles in Ocular Physiology, Pharmacology, and Therapeutics
summary: Extracellular vesicle (EV) is a cell-released biological nanoparticle exploiting intrinsic mechanisms for molecular transport in the body. EVs are protected from extracellular degradation and can deliver RNA, DNA, protein, lipid cargo across the blood-brain and blood retinal barriers, making them an attractive carrier for biomolecules and drug delivery to the back of the eye. Recent research has suggested possible use of extracellular vesicles as biomarkers of various hereditary, metabolic and degenerative eye diseases. Currently, there are expected values to use them in the interpretation of disease severity level, progression and treatment responses, and to understand cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying a variety of ocular pathologies. Moreover, extracellular vesicles may open novel treatment options and drug delivery ways.

VR and XR technologies are transforming consumer engagement and enriching fashion education by presenting immersive retail settings and digital classroom environments. Additionally, CAD and apparel simulation systems facilitate garment visualization and prototyping, improving communication between manufacturers and consumers, and reducing reliance on physical samples and material waste. title: The Impact of Mycotoxins on the Reproductive Function of Farm and Companion Animals
summary: Mycotoxins are chemical toxic compounds produced by filamentous fungi species. These toxins are ubiquitously distributed and present in all animal diets at variable levels and combinations. Most of the animal diets will contain these mycotoxins. Due to their variability in chemical composition and levels of exposure, their mode of action may vary from oxidative stress to carcinogenic activity. Some mycotoxins, like zearalenone (ZEN), are known for their reproductive toxicity due to their oestrogenic activity. However, other mycotoxins not considered as endocrine disruptors may also negatively impact animal reproduction. Additionally, most of the reproductive effects of mycotoxins are detected under acute exposure, and there is a paucity of information regarding chronic exposure.

Addressing the Transposition Challenge in Virtual Reality: Adaptive Scaffolding for Self-Regulation, Cognitive Load, and Emotions in Education
summary: The integration of immersive virtual reality (IVR) in educational contexts marks a substantial shift in learning environments, offering high sensory fidelity and interactive potential. However, as students transition from traditional physical classrooms to virtual settings, they frequently encounter the “Transposition Challenge,” losing access to familiar self-regulatory supports such as notes, clocks, and peer cues. This regulatory void, or “regulatory nakedness,” can elevate extraneous cognitive load and disrupt emotional equilibrium, hindering both engagement and learning outcomes. Recent work—guided by models such as the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL) and the Cognitive-Affective Theory of Learning with Media for VR (CATLM-VR)—underscores the need for a nuanced understanding of how immersion, embodiment, and interactivity modulate core learning variables including presence, interest, cognitive load, and motivation.

These disorders often result from a complex interplay of physiological, environmental, managemental, and nutritional factors. title: Unraveling Microbiome and Nutrigenomics Interactions in Livestock Production Systems
summary: In the field of animal nutrition and physiology, understanding the interplay between the livestock microbiome and various intrinsic and extrinsic factors has gained significant attention in recent years. Key limitations include the adaptability of decoding algorithms to dynamic environments, the robustness of BCIs in daily life scenarios, and the challenges posed by limited or noisy neural data. summary: The Central Nervous System (CNS) provides information about how individuals collect information from their surroundings, how they process that information to make decisions, and finally, how they behave and act in their environment. CNS information can be gathered from three main sources: (1) electrical currents (e.g., electroencephalography – EEG) or electrocorticography (ECoG)), (2) magnetic fields (e.g., magnetoencephalography – MEG), and (3) level of blood oxygen or blood flow (e.g., functional near infrared spectroscopy – NIRS or functional magnetic resonance imaging – fMRI). This neuroinformation is being decoded to develop neural interfaces that aim to establish, re-establish and/or improve the neural interconnectivity of CNS in order to optimize the human-environment interaction. Not only decoding of neuroinformation has been pursued so far, but also finding the best way to recode neuroinformation by brain stimulation has been of interest in the scientific community.

title: Interactions between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems in brain health
summary: Brain health is the result of intricate communication between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems. Traditionally, these systems were studied in isolation; however, recent advances highlight their dynamic crosstalk and their collective influence on brain function. Neuroinflammation, hormonal signaling, and immune responses are now recognized as critical factors in neurological development, homeostasis, and disease. Disruptions in these inter-system interactions are implicated in a myriad of conditions, such as neurodegenerative diseases, psychiatric disorders, and metabolic syndromes. As our understanding deepens, there is a growing appreciation for integrative approaches that examine these systems together, offering novel insights into mechanisms underlying brain health and disease.

summary: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's pose major challenges due to their progressive, irreversible nature and the limited availability of effective treatments. title: Predictive motor control and internal models
summary: Skilled motor behaviour relies on the central nervous system’s capacity to predict, rather than merely react to, the sensory consequences of its own actions. From reaching for a cup of coffee to maintaining balance on a moving train, every voluntary movement relies on the central nervous system’s ability to anticipate the sensory consequences of its own actions. This predictive capacity is thought to be supported by internal models: neural representations of the body and the external world that allow the brain to estimate forthcoming states and select appropriate motor commands. Forward models predict the sensory outcomes of motor actions, while inverse models compute the motor commands required to achieve a desired sensory or kinematic goal. Together, they form the computational backbone of skilled, flexible, and adaptive behaviour, and their disruption is increasingly recognised as a hallmark of several neurological and psychiatric conditions.

title: Lipid Signaling in Neurological Disorders: From Neurodegeneration to Neuroinflammation
summary: The brain is composed of approximately 60% to 70% lipids, which primarily serve as structural components. However, many of these lipids also play critical roles in cellular signaling. In particular, sphingolipids and lysophospholipids function as second messengers, direct receptor ligands, and/or metabolic intermediates in various signaling pathways. Intracellularly, lysophospholipids serve as intermediate precursors for the biosynthesis of other lipids, whereas extracellular lysophospholipids act as signaling molecules that mediate diverse physiological processes. Dysregulation of sphingolipid and lysophospholipid metabolism has been increasingly associated with the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis, suggesting that lipid signaling plays a pivotal role in neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal survival.

summary: Neurodegeneration is the gradual and progressive loss of neuron function and structure that ultimately leads to neuronal death. The hallmark of neurodegeneration is the aggregation of misfolded proteins, such as amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles in Alzheimer's or alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's, which disrupt cellular processes and trigger neuroinflammatory responses. Mitochondrial dysfunction is another critical factor, as impaired energy production and increased oxidative stress contribute to neuronal damage and apoptosis.

title: Neurobiological mediators of clinical outcomes in psychedelic-assisted therapies

Neuroimaging, electrophysiological, and molecular studies increasingly link these effects to structural and functional neuroplasticity, supported by theoretical frameworks such as the Entropic Brain Hypothesis and REBUS. In parallel, clinical and qualitative research emphasizes the centrality of the subjective, phenomenological experience to therapeutic outcome. These two literatures — neurobiological and phenomenological — have largely developed in parallel, with few studies directly testing how they relate within the same patient sample. Consequently, whether neurobiological changes are causally responsible for clinical improvement, merely predictive of it, or simply co-occurring alongside a distinct psychological process remains an open and clinically consequential question.

Under homeostatic conditions (notably during brain development), complement contributes to synaptic refinement and clearance of cellular debris. In contrast, chronic or dysregulated complement activation in CNS injury or disease drives neuroinflammation, synapse loss, and neurodegeneration. These effects have been characterized across numerous conditions, including Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), Spinal Cord Injury (SCI), Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Parkinson's Disease (PD), Stroke, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), Multiple Sclerosis (MS), and others. Recent advances in understanding complement's dual roles in the CNS have spurred development of targeted therapeutics, several of which are now in clinical trials, though most address rare diseases. summary: In the rapidly evolving field of neurogastroenterology, mounting evidence highlights the profound influence of neuroactive microbial metabolites on human brain function. The gut-brain axis has become a focal point for understanding how metabolites produced by gut microbiota, reshaped by factors such as diet, medications, and stress, interact with the central nervous system. Recent studies have delineated pathways by which short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, bile acids, and other molecules alter blood–brain barrier integrity, microglial activation, neurotransmitter systems, and neural connectivity. Despite promising insights, critical questions remain regarding the reproducibility of findings, individual susceptibility, and translation to clinical practice. There remains a significant gap in mapping specific metabolite signatures to neuropsychiatric phenotypes, as well as understanding how genetic and environmental factors modulate these effects.

summary: Enteric glial cells (EGCs) are increasingly recognized as vital communicators between the gut and the brain. Emerging evidence suggests that EGC dysfunction can contribute to the chronic neuroinflammatory processes associated with aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Despite their peripheral location, EGCs influence systemic inflammation through cytokine signaling, oxidative stress modulation, and effects on intestinal barrier integrity. title: Machine Learning and AI-Driven Biomechanics in Orthopedic Surgery
summary: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-driven computational modeling have opened unprecedented opportunities to transform diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision-making, and outcome prediction across the field of orthopedic surgery. The musculoskeletal system exhibits highly complex biomechanical behavior, nonlinear tissue responses, and substantial inter-patient variability, all of which challenge the effectiveness of conventional clinical assessment methods. In recent years, the integration of multimodal datasets—including advanced medical imaging, 3D gait analysis, kinematic and kinetic signals, wearable sensor outputs, finite-element and musculoskeletal simulations, and electronic health records—with modern machine learning techniques has enabled the extraction of hidden patterns, identification of objective biomarkers, and development of precise, patient-specific predictive models.

Cognitive neuroscience and psychology studies reveal that metaphorical language activates brain areas associated with perception and action, underscoring the impact of embodied experiences on conceptual structures (D’Angiulli, Griffiths, & Marmolejo-Ramos, 2015). summary: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) remains the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, yet it continues to evade a definitive disease-modifying therapy (DMT). Despite extensive research over the past decades, no single clinical trial has succeeded in demonstrating a treatment capable of altering the disease's course. This ongoing challenge is linked to several complexities in PD, such as an incomplete comprehension of its pathophysiology, an elongated prodromal stage, the absence of validated biomarkers of progression, substantial clinical phenotype heterogeneity with considerable symptom variability, and high concurrence of co-pathology. These issues pose significant methodological obstacles for DMTs, including the design and duration of trials, correct patient stratification, therapeutic candidate selection, the development of valid, specific, and sensitive clinical outcome measures, and surrogate biomarkers.

Visually Guided Walking in Complex Environments: Neural, Biomechanical, and Translational Insights for Neuroprosthetics
summary: Walking is a deceptively complex behavior. Each step depends on the continuous integration of visual input, vestibular and proprioceptive signals, and motor commands distributed across cortical, subcortical, and spinal circuits. Vision plays a particularly central role: it anticipates obstacles, calibrates foot placement, and tunes locomotor control before the foot contacts the ground. When this visuomotor loop is disrupted by injury, neurological disease, aging, limb loss, or the use of a prosthetic or exoskeletal device, gait becomes slower, more variable, and metabolically costly. Mobile brain/body imaging (MoBI) including high-density EEG, fNIRS, EMG, inertial sensors, and motion capture, enables in-situ measurement of the brain and body during complex realistic behaviours. These advances have direct implications for neuroprosthetics: powered prostheses, exoskeletons, and brain–machine interfaces must ultimately operate inside the user’s own visuomotor control loop.

summary: Artificial intelligence is now being investigated across much of clinical neurology, including EEG interpretation, seizure detection, stroke imaging, neurodegenerative disease classification, neurocritical care monitoring, and clinical decision support. Many studies report high performance using metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or area under the ROC curve. Yet the number of systems with robust evidence of real-world clinical benefit remains comparatively small. This translational gap reflects recurrent methodological and implementation problems: reliance on narrowly characterized public datasets, limited demographic and technical diversity, insufficient external validation, incomplete calibration assessment, and evaluation strategies that do not map onto clinically meaningful decisions.

summary: Immersive technologies, including virtual, augmented, and mixed reality, collectively known as extended reality (XR), are moving rapidly from laboratories and specialist applications into training, industry, healthcare, education, and everyday consumer life. title: How Does the Environment Modulate Feeding and Metabolism in Fish? Special Emphasis on the Impacts of Climate Change
summary: Feeding and metabolism in fish are vital physiological processes regulated by interactions between internal endocrine signals and external environmental cues. Fish are highly sensitive to environmental parameters such as temperature, oxygen availability, salinity, photoperiod, pollution, and food quality. These variables influence feeding behavior, nutrient assimilation, and energy allocation. The regulation of these functions involves an endocrine network that integrates signals from the brain, gut, liver, and adipose tissue. Hormones such as neuropeptide Y (NPY), agouti-related peptide (AgRP), CART, orexin, leptin, ghrelin, insulin, thyroid hormones, melanocortins, and insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) play central roles in modulating appetite and metabolism.

summary: Battery capacity, recharge logistics, and computational budgets are now the primary bottlenecks for scaling multi robot systems from short demos to dependable, 24/7 operations. Long horizon missions—warehousing, inspection, agriculture, environmental monitoring, and public safety—require fleets to coordinate tasks, routes, and recharge events while accounting for battery aging, stochastic demand, uncertain travel times, and heterogeneous platforms. Classical planning or perception advances alone are insufficient: persistence hinges on resource models, predictive energy usage, and infrastructure aware scheduling that closes the loop between algorithms, chargers, and the physical environment. summary: Affective computing aims to endow machines with the ability to recognize, interpret, and respond to human emotions, while embodied intelligence emphasizes that cognition emerges through an agent's physical interaction with its environment. Historically, these two fields have advanced along largely separate trajectories: affective computing has focused on emotion recognition from facial, vocal, physiological, and textual signals, whereas embodied intelligence has concentrated on perception, control, and manipulation in the physical world. Recent breakthroughs in large multimodal models, foundation models for robotics, and human-robot interaction have created unprecedented opportunities to unify the two. Emotion is no longer treated as a passive signal to be classified, but as an active component that shapes how embodied agents perceive, reason, decide, and act within dynamic, socially rich environments.

title: Cognitive–motor interactions in aging: neural mechanisms, behavioral signatures, and functional consequences
summary: The fields of motor control and cognitive psychology have been traditionally separate, but research has fundamentally reshaped this distinction. We now understand that motor control and cognitive functions are inextricably linked, sharing neural pathways and competing for limited resources, especially in aging. As neural efficiency declines in aging, there is a tradeoff between using resources to support motor performance and cognitive function. For example, older adults often display reduced performance on complex tasks due to cognitive-motor interference, compared to younger adults. Understanding the mechanisms behind this shift is critical for distinguishing between healthy aging and early-stage neurodegeneration. It will also facilitate the development of interventions aimed at preserving functional independence.

summary: The intersection of neuroimmunology and neurodegeneration has advanced considerably in recent years, with particular interest focused on the role of the adaptive immune system in disorders such as Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and related dementias. Significant studies have revealed correlations between adaptive immune cell infiltration, neuroinflammation, and disease pathology in both human samples and animal models. For example, T cell reactivity against alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta has been observed in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's patients, respectively, while emerging data suggest that autoimmune reactions may exacerbate or modulate disease trajectories. This evolving landscape indicates a pressing need for deeper mechanistic understanding, as well as clarification of the specific immune signatures and pathways involved in diverse patient populations.

title: NeuroAI and the brain: Integrating brain-inspired computational models and large-scale AI architectures with computational theories of neural function
summary: The rapid ascent of large-scale artificial intelligence has provided neuroscience with a new set of powerful tools for modeling complex cognitive functions. Historically, computational neuroscience has balanced between biophysically detailed models of single neurons and abstract, small-scale circuit motifs. However, the ability of modern AI to perform human-like tasks in sensory processing, motor control, and linguistics offers a "top-down" framework to understand how the brain might organize high-dimensional data. This convergence, known as NeuroAI, suggests that the representational spaces of deep networks can serve as predictive scaffolds for neural activity. Despite this potential, a critical gap remains: most AI models lack the biological constraints, metabolic efficiency, and architectural diversity of the brain, while many neural models struggle to scale to the complexity of real-world behavior.

Modeling Sensory Encoding: Computational Approaches to Feature Detection, Integration, and Adaptation
summary: Sensory encoding is the vital process by which the nervous system transforms physical stimuli into meaningful neural representations. Traditionally, computational neuroscience has characterized this through receptive fields and stimulus-response functions. However, sensory systems do not operate in a vacuum; they must extract relevant features from high-dimensional, noisy environments while constantly adjusting to changing contexts. From the retina’s light adaptation to the auditory system’s frequency tuning, the brain employs sophisticated computational strategies to ensure efficient information transmission. As our ability to record from large sensory populations grows, we are moving beyond simple linear models toward theories that encompass non-linear dynamics, population-level interactions, and the influence of feedback. Understanding these principles is essential for deciphering how the brain constructs a coherent internal map of the external world.

Alzheimer's disease-associated genes expression: A new direction in the ischemic etiology and therapy of Alzheimer's disease
summary: Increasing evidence supports a link between brain ischemia and the development of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Experimental and clinical studies have shown that ischemic episodes trigger the overexpression of genes associated with AD pathology, including amyloid precursor protein (APP), β-secretase (BACE1), presenilin 1 and 2, and tau protein. These changes promote beta-amyloid peptide accumulation, neurofibrillary tangle formation, and progressive neurodegeneration in patterns that closely mirror the hallmarks of AD. Despite growing recognition that ischemia-reperfusion injury may represent a critical upstream trigger for AD-type pathology, the molecular cascades linking ischemic gene dysregulation to sustained neurodegeneration remain incompletely understood. This gap limits the development of targeted therapies that could intervene at the vascular and ischemic level to slow or prevent the onset of AD.

Neurovascular Inflammation in Aneurysm Pathogenesis and Its Contribution to Neurodegenerative Processes
summary: Neurovascular inflammation represents a critical area of research in understanding the dynamics of aneurysm formation and rupture, known precursors to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and subsequent cerebral vasospasm. These events can lead to secondary neuronal injury, highlighting an important connection to neurodegenerative processes. Pathological neuroinflammation has emerged as a primary driver in these mechanisms, where initial endothelial damage - precipitated by factors like hypertension, genetic predispositions, or lifestyle choices such as smoking - initiates maladaptive vascular inflammation. This cascade involves monocyte infiltration and cytokine release, notably IL-6, which compromises vessel integrity and encourages aneurysmal expansion and rupture.

title: Molecular Mechanisms Linking Circadian Rhythm Disruption to Neurological and Neuropsychiatric Disorders
summary: Within the field of molecular neuroscience, circadian rhythms are increasingly recognized as fundamental regulators of brain health and disease. Disruption of these intrinsic biological clocks has been closely linked with a spectrum of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, major depression, and schizophrenia. Recent studies have begun to unravel how circadian dysfunction can influence brain pathology through mechanisms such as altered gene expression, synaptic activity, neuroinflammation, and impaired neuronal communication. Despite these advances, significant questions remain about the precise molecular pathways involved, the degree to which circadian disruption drives disease onset versus exacerbating existing pathology, and how these processes differ between individuals and disease types. There is a clear need for further integrative research to clarify these mechanisms and resolve ongoing debates in the field.

summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with multi-sensor payloads (cameras, LiDAR, multispectral and thermal imagers) are increasingly deployed for large-scale surveillance and environmental monitoring, from infrastructure inspection to crop health assessment and wildlife tracking. These deployments generate large volumes of heterogeneous sensor data that must be processed reliably, often with limited onboard compute and intermittent connectivity to centralized systems. Edge-AI addresses this by moving perception and decision-making closer to the sensor, reducing latency and bandwidth demands while enabling real-time response in the field. Achieving robust perception under these conditions requires effective fusion of multiple sensor modalities, lightweight models suited to onboard hardware, and architectures that remain reliable across varied, often unpredictable environments.

title: Neuroimaging for early detection and intervention in Alzheimer’s and cognitive disorders
summary: Neuroimaging has revolutionized our understanding of Alzheimer's disease and cognitive disorders. These advanced techniques bridge the gap between microscopic brain changes and clinical symptoms. Once focused on large anatomical changes, today's technologies include high-resolution tractography and molecular PET imaging, which visualize white matter connectivity and track proteins like amyloid and tau. By integrating structural, functional, and molecular insights, these tools deepen our understanding of cognitive decline. However, critical gaps remain, necessitating new strategies for optimal integration and application. Protocol harmonization, early detection in preclinical stages, and differentiating Alzheimer's from related dementias are urgent challenges.

title: Exploring oxytocin as a neuroendocrine integrator
summary: Oxytocin has been the subject of much research that has greatly expanded our understanding of its role in integrating brain-body interactions. Recent evidence identifies oxytocin as a critical modulator within the gut-brain-endocrine axis, regulating neuroendocrine and neuroimmune signaling pathways in both bottom-up (gut-to-brain) and top-down (brain-to-gut) directions. While oxytocin concentrations in the central brain are approximately three orders of magnitude higher than peripheral blood concentration, oxytocin receptors are widely distributed across many peripheral tissues. Indeed, recent studies have pointed to associations between oxytocin and gut microbiota-derived metabolites, vagal afferent signaling and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity, positioning oxytocin as a key modulator of metabolic and endocrine signals.

summary: We are pleased to announce this Volume II Research Topic, building upon the impactful contributions and insightful discussions generated by the first Research Topic in this series - 'Realistic Multi-Scale Modeling of Neural Circuit Dynamics'. Neural circuit dynamics remain profoundly complex, underpinned by intricate interactions spanning molecular, cellular, and network scales. While significant advancements in computational neuroscience have enabled the development of increasingly detailed biophysical models, the fundamental challenge persists: effectively bridging these disparate scales to achieve truly comprehensive and predictive simulations. This ongoing endeavor is crucial for advancing our understanding of brain function and dysfunction, necessitating continued exploration and innovation in multi-scale modeling approaches.

title: Global Challenges in Brain Banking for Neurology Research
summary: Exploration of human brain tissue is pivotal for advancing neurology and improving public health, especially as the world faces a growing health crisis linked to the aging population and associated neurodegenerative diseases. Traditional animal models fall short in mirroring human brain pathophysiology, necessitating the use of human post-mortem specimens to thoroughly investigate brain functions and mechanisms under both normal and pathological states. The development of brain banks—facilities that collect, store, and manage brain specimens—in different ethnic-geographical contexts and the sharing of protocols and information are critical to support the evolution of "precision neurology," which aims to integrate clinicopathological data with genomic and other omics-based methodologies to illuminate the causes of brain diseases.

Epidemiology, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Toxoplasma gondii Infection in a One Health Context
summary: Toxoplasma gondii is a globally distributed protozoan that infects nearly all warm-blooded hosts, including humans. Understanding its epidemiology and phylogeny is essential for infection management and outbreak reduction. Recent advances in molecular biology have revealed the parasite's genotype diversity and virulence factors. The One Health approach highlights the interactions between the parasite, host, and environment, offering insights to enhance animal health and mitigate economic losses in agriculture. Significantly, T. gondii poses veterinary concerns, causing reproductive disorders in livestock, which leads to economic losses and potential zoonotic transmission through contaminated meat. Its environmental resilience, supported by robust oocyst production, underscores the importance of effective environmental management in controlling its spread.

title: Advancements in the Diagnosis of Canine and Feline Idiopathic Epilepsy
summary: Epilepsy is one of the most common chronic neurological conditions encountered in small animal practice. Despite its prevalence, the diagnosis and management of epilepsy in dogs and cats remain challenging due to the variability in seizure manifestation and response to treatment. Traditional diagnostic tools, such as conventional MRI, provide limited insight into the disease processes at a cellular level. However, recent advances in neuroimaging techniques as well as the investigation of biomarkers, both in imaging and biologic tissues, may provide further insight into the disease process at the cellular level. Harnessing these novel techniques may bridge the gap between symptom observation and cellular pathology, leading to more targeted and effective therapies.

These areas are not merely human habitats but also essential refuges for wildlife contributing significantly to biodiversity conservation. Stem cells as immunological modulators in neurological and neurodegenerative conditions
summary: Stem cells elicit immunomodulatory properties through surface protein expression and their secretome. These properties allow stem cells to influence the immune response, reduce neuroinflammation, and create a favorable environment for neuronal survival and repair. Many neurological and neurodegenerative conditions involve chronic or dysregulated neuroinflammation, which contributes to neuronal damage. In these diseases, activated microglia and astrocytes release pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-1β), oxidative species, and other factors that exacerbate neurodegeneration. Stem cells have emerged as promising therapeutic tools due to their dual ability to promote neural regeneration and exert potent immunomodulatory effects. By restoring immune balance and supporting tissue repair, stem cells offer a multifaceted approach to treating neurodegenerative diseases with immunological components.

summary: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) represent the largest pharmacologically exploited receptor superfamily in the human genome, accounting for the targets of approximately 35% of all approved drugs. Unraveling the role of physical activity in brain function, cognitive processes, and behavioral outcomes
summary: Physical activity has emerged as one of the most potent behavioral interventions influencing brain function, learning, memory, and a wide range of cognitive and emotional processes. Over the past decade, a growing body of evidence from human and animal studies has demonstrated that regular physical activity induces structural and functional plasticity in key brain regions such as the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and cerebellum. These adaptations include enhanced neurogenesis, synaptic remodeling, angiogenesis, neurotransmitter regulation, and improved metabolic efficiency, mechanisms that are strongly implicated in learning, memory consolidation, executive functioning, and self-regulation.

Biodiversity Monitoring and Ecosystem Response to Non-Point Source Pollution: Integrating eDNA, Biomonitoring, and Ecological Indicators
summary: Non-point source (NPS) pollution from agriculture, urban runoff, atmospheric deposition, and diffuse industrial sources is one of the most pervasive and least controlled drivers of biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation worldwide. Unlike point-source discharges, NPS pollution is spatially diffuse, temporally variable, and frequently undetected by conventional monitoring frameworks until ecological damage is already advanced. As international policy instruments such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and national water quality directives raise the bar for measurable biodiversity outcomes, there is an urgent need for monitoring approaches that can capture biological responses to NPS pollution at scale, with sensitivity, and across freshwater, soil, and terrestrial systems.

title: Exploring the Hidden Diversity of Eukaryotic Microorganisms
summary: Eukaryotic microorganisms, or protists, are essential ecological agents that populate various environments like aquatic and soil systems. These organisms vary widely from autotrophs, which contribute fundamentally to primary production, to heterotrophs that act as vital intermediaries in food webs. While traditional morphological identification has been helpful, the integration of environmental DNA and modern molecular techniques such as metabarcoding has significantly expanded our understanding of the vast diversity and distribution of these microorganisms. Yet, despite advancements, a large segment of microbial diversity remains uncharacterized, posing a challenge to our understanding of protist evolution and their roles in ecosystems.

Virtual Reality for Mental Health: Behavioral Interventions, Therapy, Protocols, and Affective Regulation
summary: Recent advances in immersive technologies have positioned Virtual Reality (VR) as a powerful tool for mental health assessment and intervention. In particular, Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy (VRET) and VR-based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (VR-CBT) have demonstrated effectiveness in treating anxiety disorders, phobias, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). These approaches enable controlled, safe, and ecologically valid environments where emotional and behavioral responses can be elicited, monitored, and modified in real time. Despite promising results, challenges remain in standardizing therapeutic protocols, understanding long-term outcomes, and integrating physiological and behavioral data into adaptive interventions. This Research Topic addresses the need for rigorous, interdisciplinary research that advances VR-based mental health interventions grounded in clinical evidence and behavioral science.

Dystonia, ataxia, spasticity, and tic disorders — despite their distinct clinical presentations — share common threads in their underlying pathophysiology, involving dysfunction across cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical and cerebellar circuits. Advances in neuroimaging, electrophysiology, genetics, and neuromodulation have significantly expanded our understanding of these conditions, yet many questions remain regarding their mechanisms, progression, and optimal management.

title: Novel Approaches to the Diagnosis and Treatment of Neuropsychiatric Disorders
summary: Neuropsychiatric disorders, encompassing conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and Alzheimer’s disease, represent a leading cause of global disability. Despite significant research, their complex and often overlapping etiologies pose immense challenges for accurate diagnosis and effective treatment. Current diagnostic criteria largely rely on subjective clinical assessments, and many available therapeutics offer limited efficacy or carry substantial side effects. However, the convergence of advances in neuroscience, genomics, neuroimaging, and digital technology is fostering a transformative era. This Research Topic aims to capture and contribute to this momentum by exploring innovative, multidisciplinary strategies that promise to redefine our understanding and management of these debilitating conditions.

Integrating transcriptomics, epitranscriptomics, and spatial transcriptomics to decode plant regulatory complexity
summary: Plant molecular biology is entering a new era of transcriptomic precision. Over the past decade, the progression from bulk RNA sequencing to single-cell and spatial transcriptomics has profoundly changed how researchers map gene activity and regulation. Beyond traditional measures of transcript abundance, the discovery of epitranscriptomic mechanisms, chemical modifications such as m⁶A, m⁵C, and pseudouridylation, has revealed new layers of post-transcriptional control that modulate RNA stability, translation, and splicing. Together, these techniques offer multidimensional insights into how individual cell types and tissues orchestrate complex physiological and developmental programs. While transcriptomics has long illuminated what genes are expressed, the integration of epitranscriptomic and spatial data now enables investigations into how and where transcripts function, providing fine-scale views of regulatory logic in plant adaptation, growth, and stress response.

Common risk factors to comorbidity can include genetics, individual characteristics, social environment and life circumstances.

title: Philosophy meets neuroscience in the study of consciousness
summary: Conscious experience is central to human life, yet the processes underlying its emergence remain among the most debated questions in behavioral neuroscience. Over the past decade, the field has moved beyond simple contrasts between “conscious” and “unconscious” states toward mechanistic accounts grounded in large-scale brain dynamics, multisensory integration, and the interaction between perception, action, and self-representation. Progress has been driven by converging approaches, including computational frameworks (e.g., predictive processing and global workspace–type architectures), causal perturbation methods (such as TMS, DBS, and intracranial stimulation), and high-dimensional analyses of neural data from EEG, MEG, fMRI, and single-unit recordings. In parallel, experimental paradigms involving anesthesia, sleep, psychedelics, meditation, and disorders of consciousness have provided structured and naturalistic perturbations of subjective experience.

Stress, Mental Health, and the Synapse: Investigating the Mechanisms and Implications
summary: Background: This Research Topic aims to explore the intricate relationship between stress, mental health, and the synapse. Stress, a prevalent factor in modern society, has been linked to numerous mental health conditions, such as anxiety disorders, depression, and neurodegenerative diseases. The synapse, a fundamental component of neural communication, plays a crucial role in mediating stress responses and shaping mental well-being. Understanding the underlying mechanisms and implications of stress-related synaptic alterations is imperative for advancing our knowledge in mental health research.

title: Anthropogenic Disruptions and Changes to Circadian Entrainment Cues and Their Effects on Animals
summary: Circadian rhythms are an evolutionarily adaptive trait most animals possess. The circadian clock allows animals to synchronize their internal environment with the external one to optimize ecological and physiological processes for best survival, reproduction, and well-being. To synchronize these rhythms, animals use entrainment cues from the environment such as light, food availability, temperature, social cues, and other arousal cues. However, humans, through our actions, have very rapidly disrupted and changed these environmental cues. Some instances of these disruptions are light pollution, changes in the seasonal cycles of temperature through climate change, and changes to food availability through habitat destruction. These changes to external cues have the potential to cause desynchrony of the circadian system and disrupt behavioural interactions, physiological homeostatic processes, and potentially even ecosystem processes.

Alpha-Synuclein dynamics in Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms of Brain-aging
summary: Alpha-Synuclein is a presynaptic neuronal protein essential for vesicle trafficking and neurotransmitter release. While widely recognized for its pathological aggregation in disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies, its dynamics during the natural course of brain aging remain complex. Aging is characterized by a gradual loss of proteostatic control, synaptic efficacy, and altered cellular signaling. In this context, alpha-synuclein undergoes significant changes in expression, post-translational modification, and clearance even in the absence of overt disease. Understanding the nuanced shift from physiological function to pathological dysfunction is critical. As the global population ages, distinguishing between benign age-related changes in alpha-synuclein dynamics and those driving neurodegeneration is essential for developing early interventions and maintaining cognitive health.

This Research Topic will focus on brain injury as a high-impact condition in which rehabilitation is central and where inflammation-informed stratification could improve care.

title: Sensory-motor integration in human movement
summary: For desired and coordinated movements, the central nervous system integrates multiple sensory feedback with motor commands. Optimum integration of multi-sensory signals from visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems is vital to performing activities of daily life and is commonly compromised due to aging, neuromuscular disorders, and traumatic injuries. Compromised sensor-motor integration can potentially lead to a stability control deficiency, increased risk of falling, tremors, rigidity, and decreased hand dexterity, just to name a few. However, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms responsible for sensory-motor integration, specifically, how the central nervous system adapts to changes in environmental conditions (e.g., visual input is obstructed), physical and mental health, and cognitive status. A comprehensive study of sensory-motor integration can be beneficial to healthcare professionals, neuroscientists, and human health in general.

title: Impact of rare disease genes on neural development and function
summary: Rare disease genes, though individually uncommon, collectively account for a substantial share of neurodevelopmental disorders, and each one offers a distinct and often underappreciated window into how the nervous system is built and maintained. These genes contribute to neural development and maturation at every stage of the process, from initial tissue patterning and progenitor proliferation through to the acquisition of mature cellular and circuit properties. Understanding how disruption of a single rare disease gene can cascade into complex developmental and cognitive phenotypes offers valuable insight into the biological basis of disorders such as autism, ADHD, and other neurocognitive symptoms that may arise due to altered gene function.

title: Microbial Adaptation to Global Change: Bridging Scales From Molecules to Ecosystems
summary: Microorganisms play a foundational role in maintaining Earth's ecosystems by driving biogeochemical cycles, supporting plant and animal health, and regulating climate processes. As the planet undergoes rapid and multifaceted global changes, including climate warming, altered precipitation regimes, ocean acidification, pollution, land-use shifts, and increased nutrient loading, microbial communities are both responders to and drivers of these changes. Their responses span multiple scales, from molecular-level shifts in gene expression and metabolism, to community restructuring, to altered ecosystem-level functions such as carbon sequestration and nutrient cycling.

title: Transforming Genitourinary Surgery Through Advanced Robotic Systems
summary: The field of genitourinary (GU) surgery has undergone a transformative shift with the integration of robotic technology, which now serves as a cornerstone for minimally invasive procedures. Over recent decades, advancements have evolved from pioneering platforms like PUMA 560 and Probot to current industry standards, exemplified by the da Vinci system. Robotic approaches have been lauded for improved dexterity, enhanced visualization, and better ergonomics for surgeons, leading to increasing adoption. Despite their technical promise, clinical debates remain around appropriate patient selection, comparative benefits over other minimally invasive modalities, and the economic implications of broader deployment. Although early evidence points to advantages such as reduced blood loss and faster recovery, critical gaps persist, including inconsistent outcome definitions, limited long-term data, and a lack of standardized benchmarks for both clinical and technical success.

title: Effort, Attention, and Arousal: Brain–Body Mechanisms for Performance in the Real World
summary: Sustained performance in high-stakes, real-world environments places extraordinary demands on the human brain and body. Effort, attention, and arousal are three tightly interwoven constructs that together govern how individuals mobilize cognitive and physiological resources to meet these demands. Nowhere is this more critical than in contexts in which humans are expected to perform in high stakes environments. For example, military personnel, first responders, and individuals of the like must maintain peak cognitive performance under conditions of extreme stress, fatigue, sensory overload, and physical exertion. Despite decades of laboratory research, the neural and peripheral mechanisms underpinning the interaction between mental effort, attentional control, and arousal remain incompletely understood — particularly in the demanding and ecologically complex environments that are present in real-world scenarios.

The field is propelled further by the convergence of big data analytics and the Internet of Things, enabling dynamic, responsive, and highly personalized applications.
